20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;">Dear readers,</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Earlier this week, the House of Representatives passed the ill-named “Sunshine Protection Act” by a vote of 308 to 117. The law would require most states to adopt permanent daylight saving time — that is, the clocks would stay rolled forward all year, with solar noon generally occurring around 1pm. This is a great system for the summer, which is why we already do it in the summer. The problem is that in the winter, sunrise would often be very late — as late as 8:20 a.m. in New York, 8:30 a.m. in Dallas, 8:51 a.m. in Salt Lake City, 8:57 a.m. in Seattle, 9:01 a.m. in Detroit, and so forth. Marco Rubio, who was the leading advocate for permanent DST when he served in the Senate, loves to wax in speeches about the wonderful uses of sunshine in the afternoon. But the government cannot create or destroy sunshine — it can only allocate it to the morning or the afternoon. Rubio’s plan to </span><strong>“</strong><span>protect</span><strong>”</strong><span> afternoon sunshine entails forcing Americans to rise and commute in the dark, which they are not going to enjoy. How do I know that? Because, unlike most people, I bother to learn what has happened in the past.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Ignorance of history.</strong><span> Advocates of permanent daylight saving time are often unaware that we tried this before — and that Congress swiftly reversed course because Americans were </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/9bf4c776-1563-45cb-bcad-2dcad8942587?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">very unhappy about the loss of sunlight in the morning hours</a><span>. Even when they learn this, it is rare that they update their stance. Many blindly dismiss the lessons of history; they say 1974 was a long time ago and things are different now. But the main </span><em>relevant</em><span> difference between 1974 and now is that technology handles clock changes on our behalf, so time changes are less burdensome than they used to be. I barely notice them, in fact. But I </span><em>will</em><span> notice if it’s dark out in New York City</span><strong> </strong><span>at 8 a.m. in December, and we know from history that voters will notice too and they won’t be
